<meta>continues from previous page: the intellect... and the Third Article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.</meta>

Third article, it is proceeded thus: That more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universal things are prior by nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior with respect to us than simple ones, but universal things are prior <note>original: "cioza" - likely a corruption of "priora"</note>; they are known later with respect to us. Furthermore, the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls first into our cognition, and the parts of the definition are less universal, just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universal things are known later with respect to us. Furthermore, we know effects by chance and principles. But universal things are known later with respect to us. But if it is what the philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*, [we must move] from things to singulars. I respond that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition takes its beginning in some way from sensitive cognition, and because the sense is of singulars and the intellect of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, one must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act, and what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science <note>Latin: <term>scientia</term> <gloss>knowledge/science</gloss></note> through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is thus known is both known in act and in a certain way in potency, as he says in the first book of the *Physics*: things manifest and certain to us are more confused first, but later we know by distinguishing distinctly the principles and elements. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it is to know something under a certain confusion. Thus, however, the whole can be known, or that in which the parts are contained in potency, and the integral whole; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. But to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have cognition of a less common thing, just as to know "animal" indistinctly and to know the "animal" in which it is rational or irrational, which is to know "man" as "lion" <note>This example appears to be a corrupt reading in the OCR; Aquinas typically contrasts "man" with "animal" or specific species.</note>. Therefore, it occurs first to our intellect to know "animal" and to know "man," and to fall into reason if I compare whatever is more or less; as the sense goes out from potency into act, so does the intellect; this is the order...

<column-break/>

of cognition that appears in the sense. For more in the sense is divided more, and when less is known, it is more remote through <unclear>what hinders existence corporeal</unclear> and what hinders, and animal; and more is hindered the existence of animal, and what hinders, and the good, and prior the good, and so on. Or it pleases and it is evident that a child from the beginning distinguishes better and not better; and in children from the beginning they call all men "fathers." But later [he] terminates one by one, as the philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: things manifest and he who knows something indistinctly still and in potency, or knows the fiction and principle, thus he knows the genus and can know the species. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is intermediate between potency and act. And that the cognition of singulars is prior with respect to us, and the cognition of the universal is sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If both sense and intellect, cognition more and is prior, and cognition of the lesser and the common. To the first, that it can be considered in a twofold way. One way, that it is considered thus as an intention of truth. And when there is an intention of truth and truth itself, it has a relation to many things. It arrives and the abstraction of the intellect is the end here, while in truth it is posterior. In the first book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*</note> the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but also more <unclear>tonem</unclear> and he placed universals as substances, and in this consideration, it is true, more because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal existing [things] which are called ideas. In another way, it can be considered with respect to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more [universal] is prior, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For first, the animal is generated, then man, as the philosopher says in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is in the process of becoming; and in this way, the less [universal] is prior in nature, for man is the animal. Nature's intention does not rest in the generation of the animal; it intends to generate the human. To the second, the more universal is compared to the less, and it is a whole, and through the whole that which becomes more universal is not only the man and the horse, as it can be; and the less universal is contained in the future, not only the more universal, but others, as man is not only animal but rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition, and "man" is prior in our cognition, and "animal" thus through its reason. To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. One way is absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is a house. Another way, when it is parts of this whole, and stones, it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house first in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defined, considered absolutely, is known before the definition. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified by those things, but rather [by] those things that are the parts.

<summary>This page discusses the cognitive order of universals versus singulars, arguing that human knowledge moves from confused, universal concepts in potency toward distinct, specific knowledge in act.</summary>
<keywords>Intellectual cognition, potency and act, universals, singulars, definition, Aristotelian physics, nature of generation, human knowledge</keywords>
